text:
I. Enveloped in the darkness of night, with a wan countenance,
The Kisteti region appears upon its throne of sheer cliffs.
In the dark ravine, the river barks, its heart muddied with grief.
The mountains too have leaned over, washing their hands and faces in the water;
Many have died upon their breasts, they cannot cleanse the blood from their bodies;
They thirst for the blood of a brother-killer, as a man comes along the path.
I say "path," but what path is it? A narrow trail upon the cliff?
It is most difficult to traverse, one can barely move one foot past the other.
Across the way, the Kist village appears like an eagle’s nest, –
Pleasant to behold, like a woman’s bosom.
Above the village, a black mist sleeps with a pensive face.
It listens to the surroundings, its heart rejoicing in the sight.

A guest of a short time, tomorrow it will go elsewhere from here.
It will go, crossing hills and icy ridges;
It darkens, rendering the visible world invisible.
If it makes the hunter weep, lost among the cliffs,
It emboldens the wolf and the thief, those who roam in the darkness.

II. From above someone unknown rolled down a rock boulder,
The traveler looked upward, a high hill stands before him.
He listens… a little while later he heard the rustling of sand.
The traveler readies his rifle: lest it be a wretched enemy.
He gazes intently, standing with his gun in hand,
He sees a man trudging down with a forked stick.
Something black he drags head-downwards, the sand was stirred by it.
The stranger said nothing, no word comes from his mouth.
The band of his rifle glitters, like a dewdrop in the morning.
– Who are you, what living soul are you, why do you wander at this hour?
– Who do you want? I am a hunter, I do not see you as a man to be trusted.
– In what way am I not trustworthy? Why do you speak such false words? Is it because I wander like you in these rocky lands? I too am a hunter, but today I was merely roaming.
– It is the hunter's rule; are you not debt-free after all?

– This too is a debt, brother, I can barely drag my feet,
I have roamed all the crags, I left no ravine unvisited.
A black mist settled upon them, a fierce wind arose,
It howled at me through the gorges, like a hungry wolf.
I could no longer discern the path, I was on the verge of falling from the cliff,
I am a stranger here, I know not the way, and thus I suffered greatly.

In many places I startled the game, I clearly heard the sound of footsteps, or when the horn of a leaping ibex struck the cliffs. It was heart-wrenching; I could see nothing with my eyes; to say nothing of shooting or killing, I no longer dared to move forward.

The stranger approached, standing nearby,
"Victory!" he called out, "Do not lament, do not be angry."
– And to you, victory, brother, may you slay the leaping game.

– Here is the beast, why do you complain? – He showed the horned ibex,
Dead, its horns thrown back, silenced, wise.
– If you wish, let us divide it now, as comrades, in two,
I want not a scrap more, let us share it fairly.
Come with me tonight, my house is not far away.
Where are you from, brother? Tell me your name.
Do not worry, the Lord has provided food for you too today.
A share belongs to you as well in this ibex I have killed.
Why are you surprised? I am not joking, nor am I flattering you to your face.
For if it were not so, why would you have met me at this time?!
Shame on me, if I should deny you your portion.
What is your name? Tell me your name, you look like a Khevsur by your appearance.

– Nunua is my name, brother, an exile from Chieli,
– Zviadauri lied, hiding his own name.
What could he do? They knew his name; he owed blood to many Kists;
He had cut off the right hands of many Kists, and sent them prematurely to the grave.
– Teach me your name as well, for I have truly told you mine.

– Jokola is my name, brother, Alkhastaisdze by surname;
It would not suit us to speak false words to one another.
My house stands here in Jarega, with stone walls and a fortress gate.
Come with me tonight, I will lead the way myself.
If I do not host you grandly, I will not host you poorly either.
Tomorrow you shall decide, brother, wherever you wish to go.
I will tell you some of my sorrows, and you share some of yours with me.

– To reap where I have not plowed, brother – what kind of custom is this? You have cut the throat of the ibex, and its legs are skinned. If I visit you, I will not refuse; I will help you carry the ibex, but I will not ask for a share, know this, I would never stoop to that.

They skinned the beast, they went to Jarega,
They shared many stories, they got to know each other on the way.
III. They arrived, towers appeared, here and there dogs bark; curious children peek through the doorways. Houses built of slate, like cliffs, became clearly visible.
– Behold, this is my family, my fortress and my home; come, as a brother to a brother, a godchild to a godfather.

Jokola called to his wife: "Look out, someone is at the door!" –
Pride was evident in the host's speech.
They stand in the hallway, waiting...
Fire flickered upon the embers,
An elderly man sat beside him, playing the chonguri.
He sang of heroism, of the trials of the forefathers:
How they raided the Pshavs and Khevsurs, leaving no brother's blood unavenged;
Everywhere they offer thanks to the right hand of a brave youth.
There appeared a beautiful woman, clad in black raiment, like a cypress in form, a star fallen from the sky.
– Behold, I have brought you a guest, – God’s grace is upon us, – How you receive us, woman, now depends on you.

The woman offered a greeting:
– Guest, you have come in peace!
– Peace to you also, may you be kept alive with your husband and children!

IV. The man who was seen in the house, grey-haired and aged,
He too rose to his feet, like a strong mountain tiger.
A stranger come as a guest respects another’s guest,
To stand up is the custom, he cannot break the law of the mountain.
But when he saw the stranger, he took on the color of a wolf;
What he was thinking could be easily discerned.
The aged Kist did not relish the sight of the foreign youth.
His heart beats overcome with rage, and his face does not hide it,
His hand moves toward his dagger, quietly testing the blade,
But a guest in another’s house cannot stir up trouble.
He rose and quietly went out, biting his finger bitterly,
Three times he struck his hand against his heart as he stepped outside.

He went, walking from door to door, sharpening his tongue with poison:
“Kists, our blood-enemy has crept in upon us by night.
It seems Jokola does not recognize him, has not seen with his own eyes
That eradicator of ours, our ravager by force;
Always insatiable with our blood and bone,
Today he is in our hands; let us strive to give him a bitter taste,
For we have unburied dead killed by them this summer.
Speak, if I do not tell the truth, if my word is false?!
Let our enemy also know that we are not of a base race.
I am surprised by Jokola’s wits, why he opened the door to the enemy,
Whom is the shallow-witted hosting, why is he not in his senses?!
We must make vinegar flow from Zviadauri’s nose,
Or else, let us surrender our sword and shield to the women.”

The sons of the Kists were stirred, all girded on their swords,
The whole village was in turmoil: child, man, and woman.
They must sacrifice Zviadauri’s head to their dead;
They must slay him upon the grave, as is the custom.

They sent a single scout, giving him secret instructions,
To go to Jokola in a neighborly, brotherly way;
By no means should he let the village's intent reach his ears.
Let him dine, let him converse, find out where the guest sleeps;
They would attack at night, bind him, they wanted no long wait.
The spy arrived with a smooth and flattering tongue,
He honors Jokola's name, makes merry, shows no offense.
He chats, tells stories, striking his tongue like a flint.
Who knows, his heart is full of a serpent's venom and gall.

They dined. The host likes his guest from the heart. "He seems a fine brave man," – he swears by his faith: "This first acquaintance, tomorrow brotherhood, let us be joined in spirit"... He invited him to sleep, offered him his own bedding. – No, – the guest says, – I want no mattress and quilt. I will lie on the porch, I am not even used to sleeping indoors...

His desire was fulfilled, drawn from the heart,
This is what the listener wants, for this he was invited.
He went away rejoiced, informed everyone.
If he knows the rooster's perch, what more does a fox need?!

V. – What is the matter, woman? I want my sword and dagger! It is no joking matter, an enemy army has fallen upon us! They truly mean to plunder us, our guest betrays us; under brotherhood and friendship, he sneaked an army in! Hush, wait!.. I was mistaken… they are our Kists. Why have they come at this hour, what are they debating, what do they desire?! Listen closely, I hear a man’s death rattle. What a harsh noise, what a terrible roar! They are killing my guest, indeed, their daggers are flashing. Look at the shameless ones, how they trample my home! They have discarded my manhood, treading it underfoot like fruit leather, let me go and see, why, for what are they so stirred?!

Thus spoke Jokola, rose, and went with dagger in hand. He opened the doors of the house and stepped out undaunted.
– What are you doing? – he shouted:
– Whose guest are you binding with ropes? Why do you break our sacred law, why do you pour filth upon my head? By my faith I swear, I shall spill blood, I will make you regret this foolish behavior, I will make you regret, though you are my brothers, the trampling of my honor!..

– What are you saying, fool, what are you saying? Why do you not come to your senses?
For the sake of a blood-enemy guest, who would cut off their mother's breast?!
– The Kists shouted at him in unison, powerfully, with a thunderous roar:
– You and your guest, we will hurl you both together from the cliff.
Whatever the community desires, it shall do by its communal law.
Why do you keep the eradicator of all Kisteti as a guest in your house?
Zviadauri's name is known even to a child in the mountains.
He was always, you shallow-minded one, seeking to slaughter us,
Attacking us like a wolf, lying in wait for us on the road.
Jokola pondered for a moment, regret spread across his face, as if a shot arrow had pierced him right in the pit of his heart.

– It was he himself who killed your brother in the birch groves with a rifle,
We recognize his face, sharpened by rage.
"I am Zviadauri!" – he shouted down to us from the hill;
We know it all too well, clearly, we watched him from afar.
He filled Pshav-Khevsureti with cattle driven from here.
He followed the army, swift-footed, in a grey chokha.
Why do you defile yourself, you wretch, with this insatiable pig?
How does your heart not turn from sitting and being with him?!

– That may be true, perhaps… what are you trying to tell me by that,
even so, you cannot bind my heart to your desire with a thread.
Today he is my guest, even if he owed a sea of blood,
even then I cannot betray him, I swear to God, His creature.
I ask you to let him go, Musa, do not torture him so rudely,
once he leaves my household, treat him badly there.
Who has ever betrayed a guest? Where in Kisteti has such a thing been told?
What have I done so wrong that you have come to my door?
You have forgotten your own law, that is why you act wrongly;
How do you answer to my household? You are in a home, not on the highway!
Woe to you, sons of Kists, gathered at my door in a mob!
You torment an unarmed man, what does your own heart feel?

Musa (to Jokola): We shall bind you together with him, you who break the community's word, you insolent one! How dare you violate what we have decreed? You have begun barking like a cur, talking nonsense like a fool; for the sake of this infidel, you treat even your brothers as enemies. Do you not know that from this day, your own affairs will go awry?!

Jokola (to Musa): What? You cur?! You say this? Now you have made a dog of me?! – He drew his dagger, plunged it into Musa’s heart up to the hilt. – Look at the dog himself, look, how bold he has become with me! You destroyers of my manhood, do you even dare to insult me? I swear by Allah, I will crush you before you hack me down with swords, may the grace of heaven and earth strike you, for you act with injustice!

– What has the godless one done, what has he done, he has gone mad, he is out of his mind…
– Upon Jokola’s head fell the whole army of the Kists,
They bound his hands… they did not let him use his sword…
Bound hand and foot, they threw him in the hallway like a corpse,
The people’s curse is thunder, their spit – the droplets of rain.
They brought the wounded one, Zviadauri too, the captive.

What says Zviadauri? Why is his face so grim?
Rage consumes the hero because he has no sword in hand:
“Put one in my hand, you dogs, and a fine day shall dawn for you.”
This he said calmly, speaking of nothing else.
They were leading him to the cemetery, where the Kists’ dead lie,
To sacrifice him to their dead, that he might carry water for them there,
To have him as a servant, obediently, and to wash their tattered rags…

VI. Beyond the village is a hill, scorched and sandy.
Many a brave man lies there, lion-hearted and of noble breed.
At its base lies a silent slope, furrowed and clayey.
The strong heart of those who wielded sword, dagger, and rifle no longer beats;
They are devoured by the tongueless earth, cruel and insatiable;
Within it, the human form of everyone dissolves...
Neither strength nor a cunning word can save us from death's claws.
This is nature's sin, forever my grievance:
It kills everyone, the evil and the good, it has spared no one.
All passengers are swallowed up when the ship goes down!..

The sun had not yet risen, the dew still slept on the grass,
The breeze had not yet blown, nor spread itself below,
Countless men and women spread across the meadow.
The crowd was bringing Zviadauri with his hands bound,
Everyone rejoices at his killing, or who would start mourning?!
Death frightens us all, but if another is killed, we desire to watch;
Men often do not feel what a great sin they commit.
How many evil souls I know, who walk without a furrowed brow;
Or who does not desire the destruction of their tormentor?!

VII. Here is the Kist’s grave,
The people have gathered around it;
The mullah begins the prayer,
Commemorating his dead:
"Do not suffer, Darla, do not trouble yourself; we, your brothers, have come to the door of your grave; we offer you a sacrifice, rejoice, we will not let you suffer the enemy's spite."

– May a dog be for your dead! – The brave man speaks, overcome with rage, bristling like a tiger bristles its fur. The fire of a lime-kiln catches the sacrificial intent of the heart. What can bend the cloud-browed, rust-crested mountain!
They throw Zviadauri down, pressing a sword against his throat:
"May you be sacrificed to Darla," everyone shouts to him.
"May a dog be for your dead!" – he would answer the people.
A brave man does not yield, nor would he knit his brow.

The Kist sons were amazed, the people stood on end.
“He almost refuses to be sacrificed, look at the dog!” ¹
They shout, while slowly thrusting the sword into his throat.
“Let it be a dog,” he said in his throat, until they cut off his head!
“Look, just look, he does not blink an eye!”
Life fades, blood flows – Zviadauri was dying,
The enemy's hand could not kill the heart, the heart remained a heart.
And a woman seeing this sight was fainting,
The beautiful one hid her tears, standing behind the people.
She longed to help: “Do not kill him!” her heart cries out,
She thought, overcome with rage: If only I were given an axe,
If only the law of womanhood allowed me,
To let him live, and make all others breathe their last.
Blessed is she who used to lie upon his arm,
Whose breast, now cursed, used to reach his chest!
Would her love for her husband ever fade?!

The Kists grew angry, they lamented: their desire was not fulfilled,
They could not give their dead a fitting feast.
The slaughtered one cut their hearts and thwarted their boast.
The insulted ones wanted to draw their daggers together
And make windows of blood upon the corpse's body.
But they dare not, they are ashamed: "It is a sin!" – everyone thought.
The people's hearts and minds raced toward regret.
They said, as they turned back home, descending with heads bowed:
"Would we not have killed enemies like him, if they weren't doing evil?
He was a fine brave man," everyone swore by Allah,
"That is why he fought us like a tiger, he was defending his land and water.
But treat an enemy as an enemy, the Lord himself commanded,
It is better that as soon as we can, we plunge a knife into his heart."

They departed. They abandoned Zviadauri to a wretched fate. Let the dogs drag him, let the birds peck at him together; he was not sacrificed, let him lie there, that shall be his ruin. Thus the Kists shouted with pride and clamor. And the dark mountain ravines echoed that same sound.

The evening hour has come, the sunbeam descended from the mountain,
Darkness steals in, the light has breathed its last.
The sunbeams have all come to a halt, the sand glistened no more;
Nowhere to be seen, vanished is the white hair of the black mountain;
Sorrow-embroidered, the woven face of that sheer cliff,
Which is forever in mourning, with crystal tears flowing.
Mourning befits death, a dead brother – a sister’s weeping,
The forest – the stag’s flight, and at times – the wolf’s howling.
A brave man – death in battle, with a broken sword in hand,
War – the feast of the victors and the defeat of the enemy.

The turmoil and churning of the water mourned Zviadauri,
The sigh of the high mountain flowing down as a breeze.
The tears of the host of mists are commanded by God.
And by the spring, a woman – lovely, beautiful – of the Kists,
Splashes water on her forehead and chest, from time to time her heart fails her.
She wept much in silence, though from time to time she would startle,
Zviadauri's death appeared before her eyes.
She wept, but it was not open weeping, she was hesitant:
On one hand, she respects the community; on the other, God frightens her;
To mourn the enemy of Kisteti would bring wrath upon her head.
This thought belongs to the mind, but the heart did its own,
The manly death of the man would not vanish from her heart.
That image pierced the woman's heart like an arrow;
It placed the burden of mourning the slaughtered one upon the beautiful woman.
She waits for the darkness, to go and mourn the dead man by night;
She no longer thought of how Jokola was.
Whose wife mourns whose husband? What is she doing, out of her mind?!
Perhaps they are killing Jokola, and have broken down the door of his house!

She rose, looking about like a startled beast,
peering cautiously, she climbed the rocky bank of the ravine;
in the darkness, the dreadful roar of the waters sounds like a trumpet.
She approached the grave with reverence, knelt beside the dead,
sobbing heart-wrenchingly, the flat stone melted from her tears.
She unsheathed a knife, turned toward Zviadauri with it,
cut three locks of hair with the blade as a sign, a keepsake,
wrapped them in the corner of her headscarf with her slender, crystal-like fingers…

What is this sound he hears, a thundering? A ringing fills his ears…
From the graves he hears the anger and lamentation of the dead!
As if children too have begun to weep, their bitter screaming rings out!
A sound of common wrath is heard, a common heartache:
“What is he doing, the shameless one,” they lamented in bitterness, –
“May the High God strike you with wrath!” they shrieked from the tomb.
Hurried clouds were drifting across the face of the sky.

She fled, she runs, she looks back – the dead pursue her, it is true.
“Where will you escape from home, if you have parted from us here?!”
A pursuing voice is heard, the hill cries out the same,
Those standing around are not just one or two.
“Shameless!” cried the slender rhododendrons,
The grasses, the stones, the sands, lying in that land.
Look, from the grave rose her dead brother Ebari,
Peerless among his peers, a rider renowned in Kisteti.
He shrieked at his sister, thunderous words breaking from his lips:
“Woe, sister, sister, what have you done to me? Why did you strike me with fierce wrath?
You cast me into a second grave, me who was already lying in one tomb!
Is this how you prove your sisterhood, is this what your womanhood is?!”
Along the path, the barker was trotting toward the cemetery.

VIII.
– Where are you going, where, accursed one, whither do you hasten?!
Who will let you eat the flesh of a noble youth?
Dog, may your eyes go blind!
Have Zviadauri's bones become yours to tear apart?!
– Thus spoke Aghaza and threw stones time and again.
She runs and pursues madly along the edge of the rocky ravine.
She still hears the voice of the dead, the mountains echo it,
Even Aghaza's jet-black hair speaks a reproach to her.

He approached his house, light is visible there;
He wants to cry out: "Help me," to make his voice reach inside.
But he can say nothing, sweat flows like water on his forehead.
He arrived breathless and collapsed upon the threshold.

Jokola sat by the hearth, leg crossed over leg.
"Woe is me," – this she cried, the word dried on her tongue.
The husband put his arm around his wife and pulled her to the hearth.
– What has happened to you, woman? – he asked anxiously,
– Do I lack other worries, that you should now become a mourner?!
What has happened to you, what is it? Tell me, open your lips!
Did someone dare to try and force himself upon you?
Tell me, I will not let you bear that grief, I will make him regret this very moment.
The defiler of my honor, I will soon bring him to his senses,
Just as I made Musa regret coming to another's door.
– He waited for an answer from his wife, staring down at her.
And all the while he gripped his dagger, his hand resting on the hilt.

The woman could say nothing, her face had turned pale.
Jokola hovers over her, waiting for what his wife will say.
At the hour of midnight, Aghaza gradually regained her senses.
She said to Jokola: – “What are you saying? Why have you saddened your heart?
Why do you imagine that which should not be imagined?
It is all a lie… I have seen no trace of any man,
Who would dare such a thing to me? Why else would I wear this kerchief and gown?!”

Jokola says to her: – There is something else besides the Devi, my mind believes not what was said, my thoughts are in turmoil. Why have you been weeping? Tears are flowing down your cheeks; speak quickly, tell me the truth, for I can bear it no longer! Some sorrowful, heavy feeling has flown across your heart. The traces of that feeling cannot be hidden from my eyes; it is impossible for what has been drunk not to leave its mark!..

– Why should I hide it from you, Jokola, or why would you rebuke me for saying so? – his wife said to him, and a gentle trembling came to her voice:
– I have offered my tears for that friend of yours.
I felt great pity for the poor soul, dying in a foreign land,
With neither kin nor brother to take pity on him!
But when they were killing him with the dagger, he did not flinch even slightly.
Perhaps I have sinned against you, and against God too, but I wept—what could I do!..
– How could I rebuke you for that? It is better to tell the truth than a lie. You wept?! You have done a virtuous deed; who am I to judge that? It always becomes a woman to mourn a good brave man.

IX. The next morning Aghaza drove the cow toward the mountain,
Birds were descending, drawn toward the dead;
Aghaza too steals away toward the cliff above the graveyard.
From there she scares off the ravens, the vultures with fluttering wings,
The insatiable eagles, screeching over the corpse;
She keeps her hands busy and hides her eyes, shining like the sun.
From the cliff she tosses pebbles while pretending to knit a sock,
Acting with skill, so that the people cannot fathom her thoughts.

X. To Biso came the news, like a thunderous lightning bolt:
“They have slain Zviadauri, descended from heaven as a pillar,
The shield and sword of Pshav-Khevsureti, most valiant of all!”
Hearing the dark tidings, the mothers raised a wail of mourning.

In Biso an old woman was crying, she laments, sobs bitterly:
“Why am I, ill-fated, alive? Entrust me too to the earth;
Show me the arms of my son, bring them, hand them over to me!
With my son’s right hand, scatter earth upon my heart;
Woe, why am I alive? Why do I still tread upon the land?!
O dead ones, why did you not summon me to you earlier?
How can I imagine my son in the lands of the infidel?!”

The brave men heard the news, a woe to be heard,
They spoke to one another with mouths full of wrath:
"Why do you wonder that we weep for our protector with bitter tears?!"
They brought out spears with tips greased with fat,
Adorned with shields and swords, they prepare the host in the morning.
This is nothing new, let blood flow in torrents.
Apareka cries out: "You will need a week's provisions!"
"Every man must go!" – Baburauli shouts.
It is the turmoil of the agitated, do not mistake it for the sound of a flute!

XI. – Come out to the door, Jokola, do not lie quietly by the hearth,
How many people have surrounded the peaks of those mountains of ours!
They come to us as guests, they intend to pay us a visit.
They will make our mothers regret rocking their children's cradles.
They are driving away the cattle, what a turmoil it is!
The army has filled, look, the heights of Jaregi, Sam-Gori,
The rolling rocks follow the terrified herdsmen.
Go, help your own, they are running to meet the enemy,
You too go, Jokola, just as the others are going.

– Should you follow?! What are you saying, you shallow-minded? They won't let me near!
I must fight alone, let the whole host see me;
Who is loyal, who is not, let the world behold.
The Kists think me a traitor, strayed from my own faith,
They imagine that Jokola sold himself for gold,
That I am a betrayer of Kisteti, having renounced my soul;
They come and lay a tombstone upon my heart while I am yet alive.

So spoke Jokola, as he donned his armor:
He girded the Franguli at his waist, slung the rifle over his shoulder,
It is not in the Kist's nature to wear a helmet upon his head.
Alone he goes to one side, devoted to the struggle,
While others spread across the mountain to meet the enemy.

XII. The Khevsur army descends,
Bearing the banner at the front;
They headed for the graveyard,
The silent abode of the Kists:
To find their dead,
To gather the hero's bones,
And from Zviadauri's tormentors
To gouge out their eyes to the roots.

They were met by the Kist army, hidden along the ravine’s edge;
They fired their rifles, the iron-banded muskets;
The nimble Khevsur lads do not yield the way.
From both sides they fire rifles with fierce war cries,
Both are burdened by the cause, both fight valiantly.
The bullet drank plenty of blood—it grazed the mountain grass,
Yet the Kists did not break; they stand like a fortress bastion.
Baburauli advised the Khevsurs to charge sword-to-sword.
The matter came to the sword; the shield gave way to the blade,
The Khevsurs have as their prize a precious treasure and spoils.
O shield, do not fail the Gorda sword; you are its kin;
Before the Khevsurs rushing downhill, a rocky precipice appeared.

Suddenly a Kist leapt from the cliff with sword brandished,
He amazes the Kist host by repelling the enemy army.
Some thought it a deception, they spoke of an apparition:
– Who is that confronting the Khevsurs? He is on our side, who is he?

– That must be Jokola, exactly, it is truly he! – said one, and the others agreed, watching in amazement. How he does not flinch before the crowd, though they brandish swords and daggers at him. They killed him indeed, he falls, and they mark his chest with the tips of their daggers.

The Kists were greatly gladdened – "Let them kill him, if they killed him – it serves him right!
Even now he made a mockery of us, as he had troubled us many times before,
He sought to stand above the village, while dragging us through the mud.
Alone he faced the enemy host, truly he has confounded us with his glory."

The Khevsurs left Jokola for dead, atop the cliff, on Ketama. They themselves attacked the Kists, pouring down the slope. The whirling of swords and daggers began, the blows striking deep to the chest; the clashing and ringing of shield and sword rose to the heavens, unto God.

The Kist host fled, rushing toward the towers with a roar;
The Khevsurs followed behind, helmets gleaming on their heads.
They gathered Zviada’s bones in the cemetery, circling about:
Some lay here, some there, mangled by birds and scattered.

They gathered the bones in a saddlebag and turned back home at once,
Fulfilling the heart’s longing, the promise made before.
They drove out the sheep and cattle, crossed over the mountains;
They took their vengeance on the foe, what is left to sorrow for?!
At least he was not left in a foreign land, they bring their dead home,
The hope of Pshav-Khevsureti, the fortress wall, the iron gate.
Brethren will mourn their dead according to their own custom,
They will commit him to the grave beside his forefathers:
Dearly valued is the tear shed upon one's own chest!
XIII. – O mourner of a stranger, the Khevsurs have killed your husband. Go, weep, Aghaza, commit him to the grave. A raven croaks over his head, the wind sifts through his beard and mustache.

– May your enemy have such a life, for my life is bitter!
No one comes near me anymore, no one stands by my side.
I buried him right there on the cliff-top, I dug the grave myself;
Everyone has turned their back on me, everyone stands aside.
They even barred the cemetery for me to bury the body:
"Jokola has betrayed us," they say, "that is his place,
Where he fought alone, staining us with shame,
Breaker of the community’s word, treacherous, restless."
Fire burns me, brother, a flameless fire, unignited;
Incomprehensible thoughts kill my heart and cloud my mind!

The wife wept for Jokola, shedding tears frequently,
A chamois with head thrown back, thick-haired, moon-faced,
She was sewn to her husband’s chest like a pearl button.

XIV. The night is dark, a deluge falls, the surroundings rumble.
O God, look upon the suffering, help them, have mercy!
Goodness is good nonetheless – love the wretched!
Scatter the prayers and pleas of the suffering like roses upon your heart!
If you do not help, take the souls of the poor unto yourself!..
Enough of your threats, O cloud, disperse!

The river roars, rages, it crashed against the boulders,
even today it rages just the same, it knows not why it laments.
It does not fear suffering, it knows not death.
It knows only one thing: the shedding of tears, loud shouting,
perpetual joylessness, only weeping, weeping…

– Why should I live, for what? Thus thought the woman.
– In Kisteti, not even a pebble remains faithful to me.
We both sinned against the Kists; they have cursed my husband…
I have a greater sin: I shed tears for a stranger.
The water carried Aghaza away, mingling her with silt and sand.

XV. At the top of that cliff, where Jokola was killed in the battle with the Khevsurs,
Night after night they see a vision, formed like a snowdrift on the hill:
Jokola stands atop the cliff, calling toward the graveyard:
“Zviadauri, my sworn brother, why do you not show me your face?!”
From the graveyard comes a shadow, bearing shield and sword,
His powerful arms folded across his chest.
He approaches and greets his sworn brother in silence.
There too Aghaza rises, her face sorrowful and sad.
A fire is lit beside them, flickering dimly on the mountain;
Aghaza hosts them, roasting ibex meat upon the flame.
They speak of valor, of sparing one another,
Of the law of guest and host, of recognition and brotherhood.

When a man beholds them together, he cannot be satiated with gazing; but a mist shall appear, pitch-black in color, shrouding the sight by the decree of the Writer of Fate. It lies upon it like a spell, it cannot be shattered by a hammer, nor can a healer charm it away, nor can it be lifted by hand.
Only the sound of the river is heard, rushing down with a cough, and Pirimze gazes down at the abyss with her gracefully arched neck…
